However, certain superstitious people and children of this world, wishing to pile error upon error, strive to defend themselves beyond the understanding and intention of <term>Scotus</term> <gloss>John Duns Scotus, a Franciscan theologian</gloss> and the <term>canonists</term> <gloss>experts in church law</gloss> with these arguments. They claim that natural things possess certain occult powers whose reason cannot be assigned by man, just as the magnet attracts iron, and many other things which <term>Augustine</term> <gloss>Saint Augustine of Hippo</gloss> enumerates in the twenty-first book of <term>The City of God</term> <gloss>De civitate dei</gloss>. Therefore, they argue, it ought to be acceptable to use various means for obtaining health, where the most excellent and natural medicines fail; it would not be illicit if one were to procure health for oneself or another through images—provided they are not <term>necromantic</term> <gloss>demonic or black magic</gloss> or astrological—or through rings and such things.

Item, it is argued: just as natural bodies are subject to the celestial bodies, so also artificial bodies, such as images, obtain certain occult powers by following the hope derived from the influence of the celestial bodies. Therefore, artificial bodies, such as images, obtain some occult powers from the celestial bodies for the purpose of causing certain effects; therefore, it is not illicit to use them and other things of this kind.

Furthermore, demons can transform bodies in many ways, as <term>Augustine</term> says in the third book of <term>On the Trinity</term> <gloss>De Trinitate</gloss>, and as is evident in those who are <term>bewitched</term> <gloss>maleficiatis</gloss>. Therefore, it is permitted to use even their power to remove those afflictions.

But truly, the opposite is found in the sayings of all the holy doctors, and it has been clearly shown here and there. Wherefore, in response to the first point, he says that if natural things are applied simply to produce certain effects for which they are thought to have a natural power, it is not illicit. If, however, there are added either certain characters <note>magical signs or symbols</note> or any other unknown and vain observations which clearly have no natural efficacy for this, it will be superstitious and illicit. This is treated by <term>Saint Thomas</term> <gloss>Thomas Aquinas</gloss> in the <term>Secunda Secundae</term> <gloss>the second part of the second part of the Summa Theologica</gloss>, question ninety-six, article two, at the foot of the question.

<summary>This page discusses and refutes the arguments used by those who justify the use of superstitious remedies, images, and occult powers for healing. It clarifies the distinction between natural medicinal properties and illicit superstitious practices according to Augustine and Thomas Aquinas.</summary>
<keywords>Scotus, Augustine, Thomas Aquinas, occult powers, images, celestial bodies, superstition, healing, necromancy</keywords>
